\chapter{The Grammar That Is Not There}
\label{ch:zh-no-endings}
\hlchaptermodality{22}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can state the four things Mandarin does not do — no verb endings, no agreement, no article, no separate nationality word — and name where somebody is from.}

Four facts about Mandarin's shape and one join, and the whole chapter adds not a single character: three of the four are things a reader must stop doing, and the fourth puts \zh{中国} and \zh{人} together for the first time.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kàn]{\zh{看} — the verb that never changes}

\label{lesson:ZH-C22-bubian}



\begin{quote}
A new chapter, and it teaches no new character at all. Five retrievals first.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{liù qī bā jiǔ shí bǎi} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bǎi} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zì — hànzì — hànyǔ — zhōngwén — zhōngguó} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kàn} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yǔ} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hànyǔ} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: there is nothing to conjugate}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{A Mandarin verb has exactly one form. It never changes — not for who is doing it, not for how many of them there are, and not for when.}
\end{quote}

You have been given \zh{看} \emph{kàn}, \textquotedblleft{}to look\textquotedblright{}, and you have used it in exactly one shape. That was not the lesson being brief. That is the whole verb.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\zh{我看书}} & \emph{wǒ kàn shū} — I read \\
\textbf{\zh{你看书}} & \emph{nǐ kàn shū} — you read \\
\textbf{\zh{人看书}} & \emph{rén kàn shū} — people read \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The verb is \zh{看} three times. Nothing has been added, dropped or swapped.

This is worth stating out loud because of what a reader coming from English or Spanish does otherwise: they wait for the ending, decide the book has not reached it yet, and go on quietly expecting one. Spanish has \emph{hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan}. English has three forms and an irregular verb for every occasion. \textbf{Mandarin has one shape and no exceptions.}

Every verb in this book behaves this way — \zh{看}, \zh{是}, \zh{上学} — and so will every verb in every chapter after it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{wǒ kàn shū}, \emph{nǐ kàn shū}, \emph{rén kàn shū} — one verb, three sentences
  \item \zh{我是学生} / \zh{你是学生} — \zh{是} does not move either
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many forms does a Mandarin verb have? (\textbf{One}.) What changes when the person changes? (\textbf{Nothing}.) And what should you stop waiting for? (\textbf{The ending} — there is not one.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wǒ shì]{\zh{我是} — nothing agrees with anything}

\label{lesson:ZH-C22-buyizhi}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and the same fact from the other end.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kàn} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yìbǎi} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kàn} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kànjiàn} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yǔ} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hànzì} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the subject changes nothing}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{The subject of a Mandarin sentence has no effect on the verb whatsoever.}
\end{quote}

The last lesson said a verb has one form. This says the other half: nothing about the subject reaches it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我是学生}} \emph{wǒ shì xuésheng} — I am a student. \textbf{\zh{你是学生}} \emph{nǐ shì xuésheng} — you are a student. \textbf{\zh{人是学生}} \emph{rén shì xuésheng} — people are students.
\end{quote}

\zh{是} \emph{shì} is the same \zh{是} in all three. An English speaker has to pick \emph{am}, \emph{are} or \emph{is}; a Spanish speaker has to pick \emph{soy}, \emph{eres}, \emph{es}, \emph{somos}, \emph{sois} or \emph{son}. You pick \zh{是}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: and nothing after the verb agrees either}]
The thing that comes AFTER \zh{是} does not change either.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我是大学生}} — I am a university student. \textbf{\zh{人是大学生}} — people are university students.
\end{quote}

\zh{大学生} is one word with one shape whether it names one person or a hundred. Spanish would need \emph{estudiante} against \emph{estudiantes}, and would then need the adjective to follow suit. Mandarin marks none of it.

\textbf{So the whole of agreement, in Mandarin, is a thing you must not do.} That is an unusual kind of lesson: what a Spanish learner spends months getting right, a Mandarin learner has to be told to stop attempting. If you find yourself wondering which form to use, the answer is that there is only one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{我是学生} — \zh{你是学生} — \zh{人是学生}
  \item \zh{我是大学生} — \zh{人是大学生} — one shape, one and many
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the subject do to the verb? (\textbf{Nothing}.) What does a plural subject do to the noun after \zh{是}? (\textbf{Nothing} — \zh{大学生} has one shape.) So how much agreement is there in Mandarin? (\textbf{None at all}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shū]{\zh{书} — a book, the book, books}

\label{lesson:ZH-C22-wuguanci}



\begin{quote}
Two lessons in, and this one is about a word you have had since the reading chapter.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ shì} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǔ} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kànjiàn} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hǎokàn} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yǔ} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hàn} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Mandarin has no article}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{书}} \emph{shū} means \textbf{a book}, \textbf{the book}, and \textbf{books}. Mandarin has no word for \emph{a} and no word for \emph{the}, and a bare noun says nothing about how many there are.
\end{quote}

Which of the three it means is settled by what is going on around it, and by nothing in the word itself.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我看书}} — I read \emph{a} book. / I read \emph{the} book. / I read books.
\end{quote}

All three are the same sentence. If you need to say \textbf{one} book you can count it — that takes a measure word, which arrives in two chapters. If you need to say \textbf{this} book you can point at it, which needs a word this book has not taught yet. What you never need is an article, because there is not one to leave out.

\textbf{This is the trap for an English or Spanish speaker}, and it runs both ways. Arriving, they hunt for the missing \emph{the} and try to supply it from their own language. Leaving, they drop English articles: \emph{I read book}. Neither is a vocabulary problem. Mandarin does not mark the distinction here at all, and \zh{书} on its own is complete.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{我看书} — and mean it three ways
  \item \zh{书} — a book, the book, books
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \zh{书} mean? (\textbf{A book, the book, and books} — all three.) How does Mandarin mark which one? (\textbf{It does not.}) What should an English speaker stop looking for? (\textbf{The article} — there is none.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Zhōngguó rén]{\zh{中国人} — where somebody is from}

\label{lesson:ZH-C22-zhongguoren}



\begin{quote}
The fourth lesson of a chapter that has added no character at all.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shū} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shíyī èrshí jiúshíjiǔ yìbǎi} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hǎokàn} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shū} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hànyǔ} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hànzì} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: country plus \zh{人}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{中国人}} \emph{Zhōngguó rén} — \textbf{a Chinese person}.
\end{quote}

Read it again and count what is new. \zh{中国} \emph{Zhōngguó}, China, was taught in the country chapter. \zh{人} \emph{rén}, person, was the first character this book ever asked you to write. \textbf{Nothing here is new. The lesson is the join.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我是中国人}} \emph{wǒ shì Zhōngguó rén} — I am Chinese. \textbf{\zh{你是中国人吗}} \emph{nǐ shì Zhōngguó rén ma} — are you Chinese?
\end{quote}

That second sentence uses \zh{吗} from the asking chapter, and it is one of the two or three questions a beginner is asked most often.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the rule, and how far it reaches}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{country + \zh{人} = a person from that country.}
\end{quote}

That is the whole pattern, and it works on every country name without exception. Mandarin has no separate set of nationality words the way English has \emph{China $\to$ Chinese}, \emph{Spain $\to$ Spanish}, \emph{France $\to$ French}, each with its own shape to learn. It has one noun and one suffix.

The same trick makes the language name, with \zh{语} or \zh{文} instead of \zh{人} — and you already hold both: \textbf{\zh{汉语}} and \textbf{\zh{中文}} were taught in the language chapters. So one country word gives you the place, the people and the language.

Notice what Mandarin does \textbf{not} do here. It does not capitalise \zh{中国人}, because it has no capitals at all. It does not agree the word with anything. And it does not distinguish \emph{a Chinese person} from \emph{Chinese people}: \zh{中国人} is both.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{中国人} — \emph{Zhōngguó rén}
  \item \zh{我是中国人}
  \item \zh{你是中国人吗}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}a Chinese person\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\zh{中国人}}.) How many new characters did that take? (\textbf{None} — \zh{中国} and \zh{人} were both already yours.) What is the rule? (\textbf{Country plus \zh{人}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\zh{中国人} — \zh{书} — \zh{看}: the chapter with no new character}

\label{lesson:ZH-C22-practice}



\begin{quote}
The chapter closes. Five retrievals, then the four skills.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Zhōngguó rén} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{liù qī bā jiǔ shí bǎi} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shū} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kànshū} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zì — hànzì — hànyǔ} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zì} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — four facts, no new strokes}]
A character costs this book a great deal: a stroke record checked against a source, a writing lesson, a reading lesson, and a regeneration of the font the book prints with. \textbf{This chapter cost none of that}, and it is worth saying what it bought.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{A verb has one form.} \zh{我看书}, \zh{你看书}, \zh{人看书}.
  \item \textbf{Nothing agrees.} Not the verb with its subject, not what follows \zh{是} with how many there are.
  \item \textbf{There is no article.} \zh{书} is a book, the book, and books.
  \item \textbf{Country + \zh{人} names a people.} \zh{我是中国人}
\end{enumerate}

Three of those four are things you must \emph{stop} doing rather than start, which is why no lesson had ever said them: an absence leaves no word to teach. The fourth is a join between two things the book had already given you and never let meet.

\textbf{Listen.} \emph{Wǒ shì Zhōngguó rén. Nǐ ne — nǐ shì Zhōngguó rén ma?}

\textbf{Speak.} Say what you are, and ask the same question back with \zh{吗}.

\textbf{Read.} \zh{我是中国人} — \zh{你是中国人吗}

\textbf{Write.} \zh{中国人} — every stroke of it is one you have written before.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{我是中国人}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{你是中国人吗}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{中国人}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the four facts this chapter taught. (\textbf{One verb form; no agreement; no article; country plus \zh{人}}.) How many characters did it add? (\textbf{None}.) And which of the four is a thing to start doing rather than stop? (\textbf{Country plus \zh{人}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
